items.title: [bbc.com] Brazil activates protective measures after about 20 isolated Awá approach
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

About 20 Indigenous Awá living in isolation approached the Guajajara village of Tawari on Monday, November 16, in Arariboia Indigenous Territory, in the Brazilian state of Maranhão; they received yams and returned to the forest. Members of the Guajajara community recorded the encounter, and the organization Survival International shared the footage. The National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples (Funai) and Indigenous health personnel are in the area. The government activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess the situation and health risks. Authorities said they are still assessing the initial information and that this isolated approach does not mean the Awá have abandoned their isolation. The reason for the visit has not been confirmed; Survival International linked it to pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and ranchers on the territory. Local residents voiced concern about the thinness of some children and older people. There is also concern about the risk of infections, given the group’s limited exposure to common pathogens.

items.title: [euronews.com] Denmark ratifies Greenland pact, clearing way for expanded U.S. military presence
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Denmark’s parliament on Nov. 19 ratified a security agreement with Greenland and the United States, clearing the final parliamentary hurdle for expanded U.S. military activity on the Arctic island. All 109 lawmakers present voted in favor after Greenland’s parliament approved the pact earlier in November. The Danish foreign ministry must now notify Washington by diplomatic note before the agreement takes effect; it does not require a U.S. Senate vote. The agreement, signed in New York on Sept. 22 by President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, supplements a 1951 defense accord. It allows the United States to expand operations at Pituffik Space Base and establish defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, including for the proposed Golden Dome missile-defense system. The pact is to remain in force if Greenland becomes independent and reaffirms Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination. The deal followed months of tension after Trump repeatedly said the United States should control Greenland, at times refusing to rule out force. The agreement also restricts military installations to NATO members and aims to prevent China or Russia from gaining influence in strategic sectors. Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said work would begin on legislation to screen outside investment on security grounds and on plans for the new U.S. facilities.

items._excerpt: Denmark’s parliament on Nov. 19 ratified a security agreement with Greenland and the United States, clearing the final parliamentary hurdle for expanded U.S. military activity on the Arctic island. All 109 lawmakers present voted in favor after Greenland’s parliament approved the pact earlier in November. The Danish foreign ministry must now notify Washington by diplomatic note before the agreement takes effect; it does not require a U.S. Senate vote (euronews.com, cbsnews.com, defensenews.com). The agreement, signed in New York on Sept. 22 by President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, supplements a 1951 defense accord. It allows the United States to expand operations at Pituffik Space Base and establish defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, including for the proposed Golden Dome missile-defense system. The pact is to remain in force if Greenland becomes independent and reaffirms Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination (scmp.com, newsday.com, cnbc.com). The deal followed months of tension after Trump repeatedly said the United States should control Greenland, at times refusing to rule out force. The agreement also restricts military installations to NATO members and aims to prevent China or Russia from gaining influence in strategic sectors. Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said work would begin on legislation to screen outside investment on security grounds and on plans for the new U.S. facilities (defensenews.com, euronews.com). Greenland debate: Foreign Minister Múte B. Egede accused opposition party Naleraq of disclosing confidential information about the pact, and the party’s no-confidence motion against him failed (elpais.com). Next steps: Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said he expects Washington to clarify the purposes and arrangements for the two proposed defense areas (defensenews.com).

Ontario Power Generation (OPG), the province-owned utility, says the first of four small modular reactors planned for the Darlington site east of Toronto will miss its October 2030 operating target and exceed its previously disclosed C$7.7 billion cost estimate. OPG has not yet provided a revised schedule or estimated the size of the overrun. It expects to substantially complete a cost-and-schedule assessment by mid-2027. The utility attributed the risks in part to unfinished engineering work on the first-of-its-kind BWRX-300 design, which it said is affecting construction and supply-chain performance. The four-reactor project has a C$20.9 billion budget. The first unit is the first small modular reactor to begin construction in a G7 country. OPG says construction continues while it works with reactor designer GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy to complete the outstanding engineering work.

items.title: [japantimes.co.jp] Climate change intensified Indonesia’s worst wildfires in a decade, study finds
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A World Weather Attribution study published Friday found that a strong El Niño drove Indonesia’s severe rainfall shortfall this year, while human-caused climate change made temperatures during the August-to-October fire season about 1.6 degrees Celsius higher. Researchers said warming made hot, dry fire conditions about three times more likely, while El Niño cut seasonal rainfall by roughly half. Decades of deforestation and peatland drainage also left the landscape more vulnerable to ignition. The fires have spread hazardous haze across Indonesia and neighboring Southeast Asian countries. Nusantara Atlas, an independent monitoring platform, estimated that fires affected 2.88 million hectares from January through October. The Indonesian government had not confirmed that total or issued its own estimate. Researchers called for peatland restoration, stronger land protections and reduced fossil-fuel emissions. Fires were still burning, with smoke detected in eastern Kalimantan on Nov. 12.

items.title: [timescolonist.com] B.C. towns issue evacuation alerts as storm tides threaten coast
items.content_html:

Squamish declared a local state of emergency as communities across British Columbia issued evacuation alerts and closed waterfront areas Tuesday amid coastal flooding risks from king tides, storm surge and heavy rain. Squamish said the declaration would allow it to carry out flood-mitigation work. Parksville and the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation warned shoreline residents to be ready to leave. Environment Canada warned that tides could run 20 to 50 centimetres above the highest astronomical tides through Thursday. Forecasts called for up to 225 millimetres of rain on parts of Vancouver Island, wind gusts up to 90 km/h in Greater Victoria and rapidly rising rivers across Vancouver Island and the South Coast. The alerts cover coastal areas from Metro Vancouver and Vancouver Island to Haida Gwaii and the central and Sunshine coasts. Victoria closed sections of its Dallas Road waterfront seawall, and Ucluelet closed beaches and trails. The province increased highway patrols and warned that debris or flooding could force sudden road closures.

items.title: [cybersecuritynews.com] Hackers breach U.S. spy analysis network, risking exposure of priorities
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Hackers breached an unclassified open-source intelligence analysis network used by the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), exposing some information, according to people familiar with the incident. A source told The Associated Press that the breach had been resolved and involved no classified information. The network processes publicly available and commercially sourced material, including social media, satellite imagery and paid data feeds. Investigators have not identified the attacker or specified which records were exposed. Reports also indicated that the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was affected and that information at other government agencies may have been exposed. Access to analysts’ activity could reveal what U.S. intelligence agencies are tracking, even without access to classified files. Nextgov reported that investigators believe hackers used ARTEX, an AI-enabled intrusion tool, but U.S. officials have not publicly attributed the breach to a person, group or government.

The United Nations Development Programme says acting now to limit the impacts would cost $36 billion, compared with $73 billion if action is delayed.

items.title: [gizmodo.com] Tiny solar tracker records hummingbird’s 4,055-mile migration to Alaska
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Researchers used miniature solar-powered transmitters to track a male Rufous hummingbird from Alabama to Alaska, recording a 4,055-mile journey in 38 days—the longest hummingbird migration documented to date. They tagged the bird in Lillian, Alabama, on March 27, 2025, and it reached Juneau on May 3. The team fitted 11 hummingbirds with the devices in coastal Alabama and Florida in spring 2025 to track their movements across North America. The study authors said Rufous and ruby-throated hummingbird populations have recently declined; further research is needed to assess any long-term effects of wearing the transmitters.

items.title: [yna.co.kr] Doctors file complaint with UN rights experts over police hospital search
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Three South Korean medical groups have filed an urgent complaint with United Nations human rights experts over a police search of a pediatric emergency center at Ajou University Hospital, saying the operation threatened patients’ right to life and doctors’ rights. Police conducted the search on Sept. 30 while investigating a child patient’s death. The Korean Medical Association is also holding a series of solo protests and demanding a police apology and safeguards against repeat searches. It says legal authorization alone does not address possible disruption to emergency treatment. The groups asked the U.N. to seek an explanation of the search’s legal basis and recommend changes to South Korea’s investigative guidelines. They also said they plan to contact international medical and human rights organizations.

items.title: [space.com] Researchers grow potatoes in simulated lunar soil using 30% compost
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Oregon State University researchers grew potatoes through their full life cycle in simulated lunar regolith after adding organic matter; a mixture containing 30% vermicompost produced yields comparable to those in terrestrial soil. The NASA-funded experiment took place in a greenhouse on Earth and used simulated material, not material collected on the moon, so it does not establish that crops can be grown on the lunar surface. The trial used five regolith simulants and the Modoc potato variety. Researchers plan to test 10 more potato varieties and are studying growth in larger pots; the first trial’s small pots produced small tubers.
